content: The systematic review did not yield direct data from the included studies. Therefore, estimates were derived from five studies that evaluated both chest radiography and symptom screening. Chest radiography demonstrated high sensitivity and negative predictive value, particularly when any abnormality was considered. In contrast, symptom screening alone was less sensitive, leading to a lower negative predictive value. Several studies assumed that individuals without chest radiographic abnormalities and without a minimum set of symptoms did not have active tuberculosis (TB). Positive cultures in such cases were considered potentially transient, due to laboratory cross-contamination, or indicative of subclinical TB. This approach is standard in TB prevalence surveys. The sensitivity and specificity of chest radiography abnormalities for TB were 55% (95% CI: 40–70) and 89% (95% CI: 87–91), respectively, which were higher than those for persistent cough (sensitivity: 45%, 95% CI: 30–60; specificity: 84%, 95% CI: 82–84). However, there was a high risk of selection bias, as the study population included only children suspected of TB based on symptoms, contact history, or known conversion to positive tuberculin skin test (TST) or interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA). In a hypothetical population of 10,000 HIV-negative individuals with a 2% TB prevalence, using symptom screening alone would misclassify 54 TB patients as not having active TB, leading to inappropriate preventive treatment. Using chest radiography abnormalities alone would misclassify 12 TB patients. Combining symptom screening with chest radiography abnormalities would result in no TB patients being misclassified. However, symptom screening alone would require investigations of 16 additional non-TB patients for every TB case identified, while chest radiography abnormalities would require investigations of 7 additional non-TB patients. Combining both methods would increase the number of non-TB investigations to 15 for every TB case identified. The overall certainty of evidence for test accuracy was judged to be very low. The quality of evidence for chest radiography abnormalities was rated as low to moderate, while that for symptom screening was rated as very low. There was no direct evidence on the combination of chest radiography abnormalities and symptom screening, leading to an overall very low certainty of evidence. The cost of ruling out active TB in individuals eligible for latent TB infection (LTBI) preventive treatment ranged from USD 28 to 188 in studies conducted in high-income and upper-middle-income countries. Screening and treating LTBI among contacts of active TB patients were suggested to save costs for healthcare systems and have favorable cost-effectiveness ratios. However, cost-effectiveness data for various screening methods or algorithms were not available. The absence of symptoms and chest radiographic abnormalities may be used to rule out active TB among HIV-negative household contacts aged ≥5 years and other at-risk groups before initiating preventive treatment. This conditional recommendation is based on very low-quality evidence. The potential benefits of combining chest radiography abnormalities with symptom screening outweigh the harms, as this approach reliably excludes active TB before preventive treatment. However, the addition of chest radiography may increase costs and inconvenience for clients, as more individuals would require further investigations. Contacts with abnormal chest radiography findings or TB symptoms must be properly followed up and investigated for TB and other diseases according to national guidelines and sound clinical practice. Where chest radiography is unavailable, symptom screening alone should be used, offering the highest sensitivity among symptom screening rules with a high negative predictive value in most settings. Research priorities include evaluating the accuracy and feasibility of the recommended screening algorithm under programmatic conditions, developing household models to improve intervention delivery, and studying the cost-effectiveness of screening rules, including the use of mobile chest radiography.
